input.question: The Hubble Deep Field shoes thousands of galaxies from soon after the Big Bang. How is it we see these galaxies in every direction of the sky if the universe has expanded so much? Shouldn't they all be centred near one place in the sky? (i.e. near the Big Bang)
input.ground_truth: The Big Bang was not an event which happened in a particular location. It happened everywhere at once, and "everywhere" was a lot closer together at the time. The expansion is that everywhere is becoming more distant from everywhere else, not that things are hurtling away from some central point.

Okay, let’s imagine the universe is like a big, big balloon that keeps getting bigger. 

When the balloon is really small, everything is close together, like all your toys in a tiny room. But as you blow up the balloon, the room (the universe) gets bigger and bigger, and all your toys (the galaxies) move farther apart.

Now, if you look at any spot on the balloon, you can see lots of toys (galaxies) around you, not just in one spot. That’s because the whole room (the universe) has grown, and everything has spread out everywhere.

So even though all the galaxies started in one tiny spot (like the Big Bang), now they are everywhere, like dots on a big balloon. That’s why we see galaxies in every direction—they’re all spread out as the universe got bigger!
